title: Plans held loosely
standfirst: Weather is the itinerary here; everything else is arranged around it.

blocks.heading: Decide each morning
paras: Patagonian weather changes hourly and any itinerary written in advance will be wrong by the second day.
We plan capacity rather than schedule: the guide, the vehicle and the permits are held, and the day is chosen at breakfast.

blocks.heading: Both sides of the border
blocks.caption: Chile and Argentina together, crossing arranged ahead.
paras: The two countries hold different halves of the same landscape and most itineraries pick one for administrative convenience.
The crossing is straightforward with notice and doubles what a member sees in the same fortnight.

blocks.heading: Estancias
blocks.caption: Working estancias rather than lodges.
paras: The sheep stations that take guests are a different experience from the expedition lodges, and considerably quieter.
We pair one of each: the lodge for the walking, the estancia for the horses and the rest.

blocks.heading: Questions members ask
blocks.intro: The ones that come up nearly every time.

a: November to March. December and January give the longest days and the strongest wind.

items.q: How fit do we need to be?
a: As fit as you like. The landscape is as rewarding from a vehicle and a short walk as from a full day on the trail.
Ten nights minimum. The distances are long and a short trip is mostly travel.

blocks.heading: We are ready when you are
paras: Every itinerary starts with a conversation about what you actually want from the days, and works backwards to houses, guides and timing from there.
